name: Single active session
what_this_does: One phone at a time. Logging in on a new device makes it the active session and the previous device signs itself out the next time it refreshes its entitlement — normally within seconds of coming online. Last-login-wins is deliberate: it is what a person expects when they move to a new phone, and it means a customer can never lock themselves out by losing the old one.
gating: none — no screen and no feature is blocked by licence status in this phase. Phase 8 owns the paywall. The only thing this phase can do to a user is return them to the login screen, and only when the server has explicitly said the account is in use elsewhere.

atomicity.problem: Two devices logging in at the same instant must not both believe they are the active session.
atomicity.mechanism: public.claim_session() takes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the user's licences row before it reads or writes active_session_id. Postgres serializes the two callers on that row lock; under READ COMMITTED the second caller re-reads the freshly committed row after the lock is granted, so it sees the first caller's session and supersedes it correctly rather than overwriting it blindly.
atomicity.loser_behaviour: The later login does not fail. It becomes the new active session and the earlier one is marked revoked with revoke_reason='superseded'.
atomicity.lock_order: licences -> devices -> sessions, held by every function in the migration.
atomicity.lock_order_why: Two real deadlock cycles were designed out rather than discovered later. (a) The device upsert was moved INSIDE the licence lock; taking devices first and licences second would deadlock against any statement doing the reverse, and holding the licence lock across the upsert also removes unique-index contention between two logins racing on the same fingerprint. (b) sign_out_all_devices takes the licence lock FIRST even though it has no logical need to read the licence there — without it, a claim holding the licence and reaching for a session row, against a sign-out holding that session row and reaching for the licence, is a textbook cycle that Postgres would resolve by aborting one caller with 40P01: a login that fails for no reason the user could ever understand.
atomicity.same_device_guard: Re-logging in on the SAME device is not a supersession. The device is keyed on (user_id, fingerprint) and an unchanged fingerprint resolves to the same device row, so superseded=false and the old session is retired quietly as 'reissued_same_device'. This is the single most likely false positive and it is tested directly.

the_only_logout_path.statement: EXACTLY ONE code path in the app can sign a user out without them asking. It is EntitlementService.fetchAndVerify()'s `on FunctionsHttpException` branch, and it fires only when ALL of the following hold: the exception type is FunctionsHttpException (meaning the Edge Function itself answered), the status is exactly 409, the body parsed as a Map, and that Map's `error` equals the literal string 'SESSION_SUPERSEDED'. It then returns EntitlementStatus.supersededSession, which EntitlementProvider.refresh() acts on by calling AuthProvider.forceLogoutSuperseded().
cannot_be_reached_by: a network error or timeout — FunctionsFetchException, status 0, different catch
a Supabase relay failure — FunctionsRelayException, which carries a status but did not come from our function; a relayed 409 would NOT be ours
any 5xx — falls through to the cached-token path
a 409 whose body is not SESSION_SUPERSEDED, or whose body did not parse as a Map
a malformed or unsigned payload — rejected before this point and discarded entirely
a failed signature check on a cached token
a failed /claim-session call — that returns false and is ignored by the login path
a malformed session_id — /entitlement answers 400, never 409 (verified live)
the_only_logout_path.reasoning: This mirrors the Phase 2 lesson where a Supabase 500 was being reported as a network failure. An ambiguous signal must never produce a destructive action, and a forced logout of a working phone is destructive.

how_the_logout_reaches_the_screen: Through the EXISTING Phase 2 mechanism, with no screen modified and no navigation code added anywhere in this phase. AuthProvider.forceLogoutSuperseded() parks a message key and calls the ordinary SupabaseService.signOut(). That fires `signedOut` on the auth stream; the listening AuthProvider moves to AuthStatus.signedOut and collects the parked key into its existing _errorKey; the Phase 2 AuthGate redirects to the login screen on its own; and login_screen.dart's pre-existing error banner renders context.tr(auth.errorKey!) — so the localized explanation appears without lib/screens/ being touched at all.

portal_must_not_claim.constraint: Loading any portal page must never claim, supersede or revoke a session. If it did, a customer who paid on the web would be signed out of their phone at the exact moment their money left their account — the app would look broken precisely when they had just paid for it.
portal_must_not_claim.how_it_is_guaranteed: Three independent reasons, not one. (1) The portal never calls /claim-session — nothing in portal/ references it. (2) portal/lib/entitlement.ts posts the literal body '{}', which carries no session_id, and /entitlement's supersession branch requires a caller-supplied session_id to do anything at all. (3) The device panel reads with the user's own RLS-scoped client using three plain SELECTs. The only state-changing thing on the page is the sign-out button, which is a POST-only Server Action behind a confirmation step.
portal_must_not_claim.verified_live: A byte-for-byte portal-style call was made against the deployed function while a phone session was active: HTTP 200, licences.active_session_id unchanged, and the phone's session still unrevoked.

fingerprint.what_is_sent: SHA-256 of a random 256-bit per-install secret, as 64 lowercase hex characters. Opaque, and it identifies an installation rather than a handset.
fingerprint.what_is_stored: The secret itself, in flutter_secure_storage (AndroidX EncryptedSharedPreferences, master key in the hardware-backed Android Keystore). The raw secret is never transmitted.
fingerprint.why_not_the_android_id: device_info_plus REMOVED androidId in v4 and this project is on 10.1.2, so the Step 4 preference is not reachable without a new dependency — which this phase is not permitted to add. The written fallback (a random value persisted in secure storage) therefore becomes the primary path, and it is the better one anyway: strictly more private than a device-wide hardware identifier, and strictly more accurate because it identifies an install.
fingerprint.why_no_build_details: Folding in manufacturer/model/build id looks appealing but fails the wrong way: an ordinary Android OTA changes the build id, which would change the fingerprint, which would read as a DIFFERENT device and sign a user out of their own phone for installing a system update. Given the choice between occasionally failing to supersede and occasionally logging out an innocent user, this phase fails toward not-logging-anyone-out.
fingerprint.note_on_the_phase_2_value: AuthProvider's existing in-memory fingerprint (manufacturer|model|device|hardware|id) is build-level, not per-install: two identical handsets on the same build produce the same string. It is left exactly as it is and is not used for session identity.

backward_compatibility: Required and verified. An installed pre-Phase-7 APK calls /entitlement with NO body at all; the portal sends '{}'. Both keep working unchanged and receive a normally-signed token with empty sid/did. An app that has not claimed a session yet is never locked out.
canonical_string: UNCHANGED — sub|lic|sid|did|iat|exp. No format change, no algorithm change, no key change, no TTL change. The sid/did fields already existed and merely stopped being empty. Verified live: a token issued after a claim carries a populated sid/did and still verifies against the public key committed in lib/constants/entitlement_public_key.dart.

service_role_grants.before: devices: REFERENCES, TRIGGER, TRUNCATE only. sessions: REFERENCES, TRIGGER, TRUNCATE only. NO SELECT, NO INSERT, NO UPDATE on either.
service_role_grants.would_have_been_fatal: Any direct table access by the Edge Functions would have failed with 42501 — the same omission class found in Phase 2 (profiles) and Phase 3 (licences).
service_role_grants.after: SELECT added on both. INSERT/UPDATE deliberately NOT granted.
service_role_grants.why_select_only: The three functions are SECURITY DEFINER owned by postgres, which holds BYPASSRLS, so their writes need no service_role grant. The portal reads through the user's own RLS-scoped client, so it needs none either. Granting INSERT/UPDATE would widen what a leaked service-role key can do while no caller needs it, and would defeat the point of routing every write through a locked, auditable function. This narrowing is a deliberate deviation from the written grant line; Phase 8 must add write grants as its own reviewable decision if it ever needs them.

escape_hatch: public.sign_out_all_devices() via the /sign-out-devices Edge Function, reachable only from the explicit two-step button on /account. It revokes every live session and clears the licence's active session, so the next login on any device wins cleanly. A stale session id presented after it correctly gets a 200 rather than a 409 — with no active session there is nobody to supersede, so it must not evict anyone.

analyze.note: All 7 are the same pre-existing issues as prior phases, every one of them in lib/screens/ — files this phase did not touch.

deviations: Step 4 asked for a SHA-256 of the Android ID from device_info_plus. That field does not exist: androidId was removed in device_info_plus v4 and this project is on 10.1.2 (verified by searching the package source). Rather than add a dependency — which the brief forbids without stopping first — the written fallback was used as the primary path: a random 256-bit per-install secret in flutter_secure_storage, transmitted only as its SHA-256. This is more private and more accurate than a hardware identifier would have been.

The migration grants SELECT only on devices and sessions to service_role, not the SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE written in the brief. Step 2 explicitly says to grant only what is actually missing and actually needed; nothing needs the write grants, because the functions are SECURITY DEFINER owned by postgres and the portal reads as the user. Granting them would only widen the blast radius of a leaked key.

Two lock-ordering changes were made to the supplied SQL, both to remove real deadlock cycles rather than for style. The device upsert moved INSIDE the licence lock, and sign_out_all_devices now takes the licence lock before touching sessions. Without the second one, a concurrent claim and sign-out-all can deadlock and Postgres aborts one of them with 40P01. See atomicity.lock_order_why.

AuthMessages (the class holding every other auth message key) lives in supabase_service.dart, which this phase may not modify. The new key is therefore declared as kSessionSupersededMessageKey in auth_provider.dart, following the same convention.

/entitlement rejects a malformed session_id with 400 rather than letting it fall through to the mismatch branch. A non-UUID string is a client bug, and allowing it to reach the mismatch comparison would turn a typo into a forced logout.

Verification found that functions_client 2.7.1 THROWS FunctionsHttpException on any non-2xx rather than returning the status, which makes the pre-existing `if (res.status != 200)` line in entitlement_service.dart unreachable. That line is left exactly as it is — it is correct-but-dead and outside this phase's scope — and the 409 detection was correctly placed in the catch clause instead, where it actually runs.

Check 6 was run BEFORE checks 3 and 4 rather than in the written order. 'An installed app that has not claimed yet' is only true of a licence with no active session, which stops being the case the moment check 3 claims one; running it in the written order would have asserted empty sid/did against a licence that legitimately had them, testing the wrong thing entirely.
test_hygiene: Every live check ran against the real deployed stack with a throwaway auth user, which was deleted afterwards. FK cascade verified: 0 devices, 0 sessions, 0 licences left behind.

extra_false_positive_closed: A cross-user false positive was found while tracing the sign-out path and fixed. EntitlementService.clear() now drops the stored session id along with the cached token. Previously the id survived a sign-out, so the NEXT user to sign in on the same phone would carry the previous user's session id on their first /entitlement call, before their own claim had landed. Harmless for a brand-new user, but a user who was already signed in on another phone would not match their own active session — the server would correctly answer 409 and this app would have signed them out moments after they successfully signed in. Neither the device secret nor last_known_server_time is cleared: both are statements about the DEVICE, not the user.
